children.translated_text: observing the skill in the art of enchantment and seeing [her readiness] —

children.text: sadyo yāvaka-maṇḍanaṃ na racitaṃ pāde kuraṅgī-dṛśā
children.translated_text: the lac-ornament was not yet applied to the feet by the doe-eyed one,

children.text: smerāntā viśada-cchade ca śayane dṛṣṭiḥ samāropitā
children.translated_text: yet with a smiling glance she cast her gaze upon the bed with its bright sheet.
The beloved is embraced without a gap, is kissed again and again;

children.text: tad bāḍhaṃ kriyate yad asya rucitaṃ cāṭūccakais tanyate
children.translated_text: whatever pleases him is eagerly done, and the sweetest blandishments are spread —

children.text: sakhyā mugdha-vadhūr iyaṃ rati-vidhau yatnena saṃśikṣitā
children.translated_text: this innocent bride was carefully instructed in the art of love by her friend;

children.text: nribhrāntaṃ guruṇā punaḥ śata-guṇaṃ puṣpeṣuṇā kāritā
children.translated_text: but [even] without bewilderment, she was made [to perform] a hundredfold by the mighty master — <s>Puṣpeṣu</s> (the Flower-arrowed one, Kāma).
'O handsome one, by the blessed [god of love], even in the blazing fire of love burning in her dear heart,
her steadfast devotion has long revealed the excess of her love;

children.text: tava tu hṛdaye śīte'py evaṃ sadaiva sukhāptaye
children.translated_text: but in your heart, though cold, even so — always, for the sake of happiness,

children.text: mama sahacarī sā niḥsnehā manāg api na sthitā
children.translated_text: my companion has not remained even slightly without affection [toward you].'

children.text: ko'yaṃ vimuñca kuru nātha vaco madīyam
children.translated_text: 'Who is this? Release [her]! Do my bidding, O lord;
console the slender-limbed one, wasted by the fire of love;
alone, [struck] by the splendor of the harsh king of stars (the moon),

children.text: pañcatvam āśu nanu yāsyati sā varākī
children.translated_text: will she not swiftly reach death, the wretched one?'
'I am placing this garment here on this tree;
you two stay right here, quietly' —
having spoken thus to the lovers in their private place,
the skilled friend herself went behind the creepers.

children.text: sphurati yad idam uccair locanaṃ tanvi vāmaṃ
children.translated_text: 'When this left eye throbs intensely, O slender one,
and the slope of your breasts displays a lovely line of horripilation,
and the thigh-stalk trembles within —

children.text: nanu vadati tad adya preyasā saṃgamaṃ te
children.translated_text: surely all this proclaims your union with your beloved today!'
Thus and in other ways, the friends
always perform various services;
like the vessel-treasuries containing the entire
secret counsel of women.
Thus is this <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment)
to be always composed by poets;
a poem devoid of it
is generally said to be lacking in <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic savor).
Having considered thus, the connoisseur of <s>rasa</s>
who composes this sentiment with abundant devices —
that poem, mounting the lips of the learned,
wanders throughout the world.

children.text: iti śrī-rudra-bhaṭṭa-viracite śṛṅgāra-tilakābhidhāne kāvya-rasālaṅkāre vipralambho nāma dvitīyaḥ paricchedaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the second chapter, called <s>Vipralambha</s> (Separation), in the <s>Śṛṅgāratilaka</s>, the treatise on poetic <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s>, composed by <s>Śrī Rudrabhaṭṭa</s>.
Third Chapter
From distorted limbs, speech, actions,
and costumes, there arises a <s>rasa</s>
called <s>hāsya</s> (the comic), because it is rooted in laughter;
it resides in three types of characters, as follows:
With cheeks slightly expanded,
eyes slightly widened,
teeth slightly visible — thus it is
in the case of superior characters, as follows:

children.text: pāṇau kaṅkaṇam utphaṇaḥ phaṇipatir netraṃ jvalat-pāvakaṃ
children.translated_text: A serpent-king with raised hood as a bracelet on his hand; eyes of blazing fire;
a neck twisted with the stiffened <s>kālakūṭa</s> (deadly) poison; an elephant-skin as garment —
'This fine attire of the Lord is [worn] to charm the eyes of <s>Gaurī</s>!' — this thought of mine:
may the arising of laughter of <s>Paśupati</s> (Śiva), manifested by the blooming of his cheeks, protect you!
For the middling characters, this [laughter] arises
with the lotus of the mouth fully open;
for the low characters, with tears falling,
with audible sound — as follows:

children.text: mugdhe tvaṃ subhage na vetsi madana-vyāpāram adyāpi taṃ
children.translated_text: 'O innocent one, O beautiful one, you do not yet know this manner of <s>Madana</s> (Love);

children.text: nūnaṃ te jalajaiṣiṇāyam alinā dṛṣṭo na bhartādharaḥ
children.translated_text: surely this bee, seeking lotuses, has not [yet] seen your lord's lip!' —

children.text: sakhyaivaṃ hasitaṃ vadhūṃ prati tathā sānandam āvirbhavad
children.translated_text: When the friend laughed thus addressing the bride, [the bees came] as if
racing, drawn by the fragrance of wine within [her] mouth.

children.text: tyaktvā guñja-phalāni mauktikamayī bhūṣā staneṣv āhitā
children.translated_text: 'Leaving aside berry-ornaments, pearl jewelry is placed upon the breasts;

children.text: strīṇāṃ kaṣṭam idaṃ kṛtaṃ sarasijaṃ karṇe na barhi-cchadam
children.translated_text: how cruel to women! A lotus in the ear, not a peacock-feather!' —

children.text: itthaṃ nātha tavāridhāmni śavarair ālokya citra-sthitiṃ
children.translated_text: Thus, O lord, in your enemy's abode, having seen the peculiar arrangement [of ornament-wearing] by the <s>Śabaras</s> (tribals),
they laugh aloud together with their wives, their eyes moist with tears [of laughter].
Herein arise: striking by the friend's hand,
rolling of the eyes, bodily contortions,
twitching of the nose and cheeks,
and flushing of the face.
<s>Karuṇa</s> (the pathetic) is to be known as having grief as its essence,
arising from the loss of loved ones, servants, or wealth;
therein the hero, struck by fate,
becomes a vessel of sorrow — [as follows]:

children.text: bhartā saṃgara eva mṛtyu-vasatiṃ prāptaḥ samaṃ bandhubhir
children.translated_text: 'My husband has reached the abode of death in battle itself, along with his kinsmen;

children.text: yūnāṃ kāmam iyaṃ dunoti ca mano vaidhavya-bhāvād vadhūḥ
children.translated_text: this bride, through her widowhood, torments the minds of young men;

children.text: bālo dustyaja eka eva ca śiśuḥ kaṣṭaṃ kṛtaṃ vedhasā
children.translated_text: the boy is small, and the single child is hard to abandon — cruel is the work of the Creator;
"I shall live!" — thus laments the wife of your enemy, O king.'
Falling to the ground, blaming fate,
weeping, pitiful cries,
striking the body, fainting,
and change of color arise herein.
<s>Raudra</s> (the furious) has anger as its essence,
[directed] against enemies, out of indignation;
the hero therein is predominantly <s>rākṣasa</s>-like,
of exceedingly fierce combat.

children.text: yaḥ prāṇāpahatiḥ kṛtā mama pituḥ kṣudrair yudhi kṣatriyai
children.translated_text: 'The slaying of my father was committed by those base <s>kṣatriyas</s> in battle;

children.text: rāmo'haṃ ramaṇīr vihāya balavan niḥśeṣam eṣāṃ haṭhāt
children.translated_text: I am <s>Rāma</s> (Paraśurāma) — abandoning pleasures, I shall forcibly and utterly [destroy] them all;
with necks severed by the blows of my brilliant and mighty axe-edge,
with streams of foul blood flowing within the currents — I shall satisfy my fury!'
Flushing of the face, brandishing of weapons,
perspiration, trembling, biting the lip,
boasting of one's power, striking with the hand,
and frowning arise herein.
<s>Vīra</s> (the heroic) has enthusiasm as its essence,
preceded by compassion, generosity, or battle;
it is threefold; the hero therein
arises endowed with <s>sattva</s> (fortitude).
Adorned with gravity, magnanimity, beauty,
valor, steadfastness, and the rest;
having won over people; with prowess of proven
and accomplished valor in battle.
'O bird, wretched one, soothe the dove;
hold steady — [take] my flesh!

children.text: śibir ahaṃ bhavatā vidito na kiṃ
children.translated_text: I am <s>Śibi</s> — am I not known to you,
capable of rescuing all beings?'
'You are happy indeed, O <s>Hari</s>,
being satisfied with the mere attainment of the three worlds;
I am <s>Bali</s>, the giver to supplicants —
nothing more was even asked of me!'
'What was made to seem [soft as] castor stalks by the fierce mace-like tusks of <s>Airāvaṇa</s>,
what was made to seem [soft as] lotus stems even by the thunderbolt scattering streaks of fire —

children.text: mad-vakṣasy avalambya kiṃcid adhunā tad vismṛtaṃ vajriṇā
children.translated_text: resting upon my chest — now that has been forgotten by the Thunderbolt-wielder (<s>Indra</s>);

children.text: yuddhaṃ yady avalambate sa tu punaḥ sajjo'smy ahaṃ rāvaṇaḥ
children.translated_text: if he takes up battle again, I, <s>Rāvaṇa</s>, am ready!'
Firmness, pride, haughtiness, intelligence, remembrance, horripilation arise herein,
as well as various verbal challenges, and impulses of enthusiasm and indignation. //
<s>Bhayānaka</s> (the terrible) — the permanent emotion
of fear becomes this <s>rasa</s>;
arising from distorted sounds and the like,
[with] children, women, or low characters as the hero — as follows:
Hearing the sound of drums at the door, with arms gracefully trembling in fright,
the innocent child, dusty all over, clings to the neck of the fortunate [father]. //
Cast away by the angry one during a quarrel of love,
though he had displayed the utmost flattery, though he had bowed at her lotus-feet —
at the roar of a fresh rain-cloud, that frightened woman
embraced her lord, snapping her trembling pearl necklace.
'With all limbs arrested by trembling,
with drops of perspiration streaming down —
by those enemies of yours, O lord of the earth,
that you set in motion — they have been made womanly!'
Change of color, tears, terror,
trembling of hands, feet, and the like,
perspiration, drying of the mouth, looking in all directions,
and agitation are declared [as its components].
<s>Bībhatsa</s> (the loathsome) is to be known as having disgust as its nature,
arising from the sight of unpleasant [things],
or from hearing, or from mention,
or from putrid and similar objects — as follows:
With rolling worms and corpses, fragrant with flowing blood and fat,
accompanied by the fierce smell spreading from rows of decomposing bodies,
with abundant vultures circling about, skilled in the dance-art of the torso's twisting —
the cremation ground of the dead shone forth, having <s>Kauṇapa</s> (flesh-eating demons) accomplished in [its] qualities.
Covering the nose, contortion of the face,
concealment of the body,
spitting and the like arise herein,
from revulsion even in superior persons.
<s>Adbhuta</s> (the marvelous) is to be known by connoisseurs of <s>rasa</s>
as having wonder as its essence,
arising from magic, conjuring, divine women,
forests, and the like — as follows:
'Truly, O swan, you have stolen this gait of women;
[yet] they still wander about;
nevertheless, this —
that is wondrous magic!'
Faltering of speech, exclamations of 'Well done!', and
perspiration, horripilation, and trembling,
steadiness and reddening of the gaze,
and blossoming [of the face] arise here.
<s>Śānta</s> (the tranquil [rasa]) arises from perfect knowledge,
through equanimity toward all beings;
the hero there is one free from desire,
due to the decay of darkness and passion.

children.text: dhanam aharahar dattaṃ svīyaṃ yathārthitam arthine
children.translated_text: Wealth was given day after day, one's own, as requested to the supplicant;
the enemy clan was reduced to [only their] women remaining, by the flourishing of one's own sword;

children.text: praṇayini jane rāgodrikte ratir vihitā ciraṃ
children.translated_text: to beloved people, in whom affection surges, love was given for a long time—

children.text: kim aparam ataḥ kartavyaṃ nas tanāv api nādaraḥ
children.translated_text: what else remains to be done by us? Even for the body there is no concern.
The mind here, without support,
rests firmly in the Self alone;
there is no desire for pleasure, and likewise
no agitation arises even in suffering.
The eight <s>rasas</s> (sentiments) mentioned previously—
among them it is established that
two by two are mutually opposed <s>rasas</s>;
one should avoid their conjunction.
<s>Śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic) and <s>bībhatsa</s> (disgusting),
likewise <s>vīra</s> (heroic) and <s>bhayānaka</s> (terrifying),
<s>raudra</s> (furious) and <s>adbhuta</s> (wondrous), and <s>hāsya</s> (comic)
and <s>karuṇa</s> (pathetic) are enemies of each other.
<s>Hāsya</s> (comic) arises from <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic);
<s>karuṇa</s> (pathetic) from the activity of <s>raudra</s> (furious);
<s>adbhuta</s> (wondrous) likewise from <s>vīra</s> (heroic);
and <s>bhayānaka</s> (terrifying) from <s>bībhatsa</s> (disgusting).
Those that are called effect and cause—
these [pairs of] <s>rasas</s> declared by the wise—
even when their combination is made skillfully,
it is certainly not a fault.
Certain <s>bhāvas</s> (emotional states) that were shown earlier
in the divisions of <s>rasa</s>
are here described independently—
they are considered delightful by the accomplished.
These <s>bhāvas</s> beginning with <s>rati</s> (love)
are indicators of the intent of <s>rasa</s>;
[they number] fifty—<s>sthāyin</s> (permanent), <s>saṃcārin</s> (transitory),
and <s>sāttvika</s> (temperamental)—know them.
In <s>rasas</s> such as <s>śṛṅgāra</s> etc.,
the <s>bhāvas</s> beginning with <s>rati</s> are considered [permanent];
individually, due to their permanence; and others—
thirty-three—are considered transitory (<s>cara</s>).
Generally, when the mind is in an unsettled state,
the <s>bhāvas</s> that arise are of mixed origin;
[they are described here] for the most part,
yet these are as they are established:
Apprehension, jealousy, fear, languor,
sickness, anxiety, recollection, fortitude,
longing, astonishment, joy,
bashfulness, madness, and likewise intoxication,
despondency, stupor, sleep,
dissimulation, and fickleness—these
are the <s>bhāvas</s> to be employed
as transitory states (<s>vyabhicārin</s>) in <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic rasa).
Fatigue, fickleness, sleep,
dreaming, and languor likewise,
apprehension, jealousy, and dissimulation—
these are the <s>bhāvas</s> that occur in <s>hāsya</s> (the comic rasa).
Wretchedness, anxiety, and languor,
world-weariness, stupor, and recollection,
and sickness—these should be known as
the <s>bhāvas</s> in <s>karuṇa</s> (the pathetic rasa) by those learned in emotional states.
Joy, jealousy, and pride,
enthusiasm, and intoxication itself,
fickleness, ferocity, and impetuosity—
these are declared as the <s>bhāvas</s> in <s>raudra</s> (the furious rasa).
Impatience, awakening,
conjecture, and deliberation, fortitude,
anger, jealousy, tears, bewilderment,
agitation, and horripilation,
pride, intoxication, and fierceness—
these are the <s>bhāvas</s> that occur in <s>vīra</s> (the heroic rasa).
Terror and death also
are to be mentioned in <s>bhayānaka</s> (the terrifying rasa).
Epilepsy, despair,
fear, impetuosity, deliberation, intoxication,
and madness—these should be known
as the <s>bhāvas</s> arising from <s>bībhatsa</s> (the disgusting rasa).
Agitation, stupor, delusion,
astonishment, delight, and deliberation—
these <s>bhāvas</s> the wise ones assign
to this <s>adbhuta</s> (wondrous) rasa.
Thus the transitory <s>bhāvas</s>
should be known as established for each <s>rasa</s>;
but the <s>sāttvika</s> (temperamental) ones—these
all belong to all <s>rasas</s>.
That speech which is rich in dance, song, the enjoyment of pleasures,
dress, physical beauty, enumeration [of qualities], and charming composition,
delightful with sweetness and lovely with brief compounds—
that is known here as the <s>kaiśikī</s> [style].
For the enhancement of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic),
<s>hāsya</s> (comic), and <s>karuṇa</s> (pathetic) <s>rasas</s>,
this <s>vṛtti</s> (style) should be employed
with effort by the wise, as [prescribed].

children.text: saundaryaṃ śaśa-lāñchanasya kavibhir mithyaiva tad varṇyate
children.translated_text: The beauty of the hare-marked [moon] is described by poets only falsely;
where is the charm of the lotus, whose luster is broken by the night's enjoyment?
Having pondered this long, the doe-eyed one, rich in the splendor of loveliness,
looks — at her own face, [raised] with new youthful pride — I think [she looks at] her two breasts.
The graceful eye is an arrow in the hand of the flower-armed [Love-god], the splendor of passion,
the sole abode of fortune, the touchstone of coquetry, the banner of accomplished skill;
this is the evidence, friend — a new nail-mark in the armpit
of some secret treasure-house of sport, a kinsman of intoxication — let it be concealed with the garment!
In those [faces] where the radiance of gleaming golden earrings,
brilliant as it was, sufficed only to cause torment—
in those lotus-faces of charming women,
fierce fires blazed abundantly.
That which is rich in varied combat, whirling, weapon-strikes,
magical illusions, leaping, and jumping,
vigorous, heavy in syllables, tight in composition—
this style should be known by the wise as <s>ārabhaṭī</s>.
In the <s>raudra</s> (furious), <s>bhayānaka</s> (terrifying),
and <s>bībhatsa</s> (disgusting) [rasas], by the discerning,
this style, which beautifies poetry,
is thus to be employed.
Pearls flowing from elephant-frontal-globes split by weapons, stained with blood;
a vast, quivering brilliance creating a great shimmering quadrangle;
sword-tips gleaming atop steady war-elephants charging forth in fury, seized with fierce determination—
the battle, with warriors grasped by <s>siddha</s>-women, then became irresistible.

children.text: nāyaṃ garji-ravo gabhīra-paruṣaṃ tūryaṃ tadīyaṃ tv idaṃ
children.translated_text: This is not the rumbling of thunder; that deep and harsh [sound] is [rather] his war-drum;
these are not clouds with the splendor of terrible serpent-bodies — this is his army's dust;
thus, O lord, in the season of fresh rain-clouds, the enemy's wives,
bewildered with doubt about your army, with wilting facial luster, tremble and perish.
Drinking blood, savoring flesh,
dragging a garland of entrails,
in the battlefield crowded with headless torsos,
this jackal roams about in the great war.
That whose activity is predominated by joy and superior <s>sattva</s> (nobility),
charming with noble speech marked by generosity,
and graced by wonderful prosperity—
that is considered here the style called <s>sātvatī</s>.
Not overly abstruse in wealth of meaning,
pleasing to the ear and delighting the mind—
in <s>vīra</s> (heroic), <s>raudra</s> (furious), <s>adbhuta</s> (wondrous), and <s>śānta</s> (tranquil),
this style is considered [appropriate] as follows.

children.text: lakṣmyās tvaṃ janako nidhiś ca payasāṃ niḥśeṣa-ratnākaro
children.translated_text: You are the father of <s>Lakṣmī</s>, the treasure and the ocean of waters, the complete mine of gems;

children.text: maryādā-niratas tvam eva jaladhe brūte'tra ko'nyādṛśam
children.translated_text: O ocean, you alone are devoted to boundaries — who else can say as much?

children.text: kiṃ tv ekasya gṛhaṃ gatasya baḍavā-vahneḥ sadā tṛṣṇayā
children.translated_text: But that you cannot bear to fill even the belly of the <s>vaḍavā</s>-fire,

children.text: klāntasyodara-pūraṇe'pi na saho yat tan manāṅ madhyamam
children.translated_text: which has entered your home, always thirsting, and is exhausted — that is somewhat middling.
With gaping, prominent, hard pupils scattered with streams of fire-sparks, [flashing] in fury,
the gaze of the sun-garlanded one, eager for the desired battle, blazed like an ill-omened lightning-bolt.

children.text: atyadbhutaṃ narādhipa tava kīrtir dhavalayanty api jaganti &
children.translated_text: Most wondrous, O king — your fame, though whitening the worlds,

children.text: raktān karoti suhṛdo malinayati ca vairi-vadanāni //
children.translated_text: yet makes friends devoted [red] and causes the faces of enemies to become soiled [dark].
With attachment to sense-objects long ceased,
for a very long time now,
the mind desires only
absorption in the Self alone.
Predominated by chief characters (<s>pradhāna-puruṣa</s>),
filled with fine oblique speech (<s>vakrokti</s>)—
this would be the <s>bhāratī</s> style,
having <s>vīra</s> (heroic), <s>hāsya</s> (comic), and <s>adbhuta</s> (wondrous) as its basis.
Birth, body, death, bondage, and the like—
these are equal, the same as for others, among good people;
that nevertheless [they attain] vast and mountain-like fortunes—
the cause of that is solely their daring.
May the laughter of <s>Hari</s> purify you—
who was guarded by <s>Yaśodā</s>, who punishes those hostile to the world,
whose laughter in childhood was
restrained yet profound.
This king, though fearless, in battle
gives that to the enemies—
spotless fame is [received] by those unworthy,
and he takes this [away] — how wondrous!
Having beheld these charming styles thus,
and having seen the compositions of great poets,
observing this variety, the poet should compose
poetry that steals the hearts of good people.
Flavorless (<s>virasa</s>), opposed in sentiment (<s>pratyanīka</s>),
ill-joined in <s>rasa</s> (<s>duḥsandhāna</s>),
juiceless (<s>nīrasa</s>), and with unfitting characters (<s>pātra-duṣṭa</s>)—
such poetry is not praised by the good.
'Abandoning the grief of your mother's death,
O innocent one, honor your youth with me explicitly'—
this and the like
is considered <s>virasa</s> (flavorless).
Where in a composition a single <s>rasa</s>
is carried on continuously without interruption
desiring great elaboration—
some [consider] that too as <s>nīrasa</s> (juiceless).
'Stinking [pus] oozing from nail-scratches,
flooding the cheek-surface, in lovemaking—
I drink the face of that [woman]'—
that is called <s>pratyanīka</s> (opposed in sentiment).
'Go to that same unfitting woman
who is inflamed on your account;
what business have you with me, rogue?'—
this is <s>duḥsandhāna-rasa</s> (ill-joined in sentiment).
'A villain is the beloved; the mind is wilted; <s>Manobhava</s> (Love-god)
[makes her] emaciated; tormented by separation'—
this
and the like pertaining to her is <s>nīrasa</s> (juiceless).
'A naive woman without pretense; a courtesan
who is a maiden; she is skilled in love;
a family woman who is always bold'—
this is considered <s>pātra-duṣṭa</s> (unfitting characterization).
In other <s>rasas</s> too, these
faults should be avoided by the wise,
because of which poetry does not attain
a succession of <s>rasas</s>.
By this path described by me,
which has encompassed the complete variety of <s>rasa</s>,
the Goddess of Speech, adorned with graceful feet and words,
becomes a beloved woman for the accomplished.
This treatise named <s>Śṛṅgāratilaka</s>
(The Ornamental Mark of Love) was composed by me;
may poets and lovers
study it for their cultivation.
What is a tale of poetry? What manner of
wit? What is the attainment of <s>rasa</s>?
What is the ornament of assemblies?—Alas,
without the <s>Śṛṅgāratilaka</s>!

children.text: tripura-vadhād eva gatām ullāsam umāṃ samasta-deva-natām &
children.translated_text: Having delighted <s>Umā</s>, who is worshipped by all the gods, [she who had been distressed] since the destruction of <s>Tripura</s>,
<s>Rudra</s> propitiates [her] once again through the method of the <s>Śṛṅgāratilaka</s>.

children.text: iti śrī-rudra-bhaṭṭa-viracite śṛṅgāra-tilakābhidhāne kāvya-rasālaṅkāre hāsyādi-rasa-nirūpaṇaṃ nāma tṛtīyaḥ paricchedaḥ
children.translated_text: Thus ends the Third Chapter, entitled 'The Examination of <s>Hāsya</s> and Other <s>Rasas</s>,' in the <s>Śṛṅgāratilaka</s>, a treatise on poetic <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṅkāra</s>, composed by the illustrious <s>Rudrabhaṭṭa</s>.
